excerpt: Rindler runs repetitive web work on the portals your team logs into, such as pulling records and submitting forms, from plain-English tasks. $1 per finished run.
content:
Rindler automates the web work teams still do by hand on sites that have no API: signing into portals to pull records, download statements, check claim or order status and submit forms. You describe the task in plain English; Rindler goes to the real site, signs in when needed, completes the task and returns structured data, and you can put it on a schedule. Instead of a browser agent working out each page every time, Rindler maps each site ahead of time (its makers say more than 1,000 sites at launch) and repairs the map when pages change, so the same fields come back every run.

You set rules for what it may never do; the launch images show paying, changing card details and similar actions switched off, with every refusal logged. Developers can call it over an MCP server. Pricing is per finished run, $1 each, with monthly plans from $100.

Rindler was founded in 2025 by MIT classmates and is backed by Y Combinator, according to its site. The makers on Product Hunt are Michael Serrano and co-founder and CTO Arthur De Los Santos. Rindler launched there on 7 August 2026, hunted by Garry Tan, and finished #3 for the day with 235 upvotes and 21 comments (as of 14 October 2026). In October 2026 Rindler's home page pointed visitors to Maxxwell, a new product the team is building, while its product, pricing and FAQ pages remained online.

We have not tested Rindler ourselves. This page brings together its official site, pricing, About and FAQ pages, its Product Hunt launch and the public pricing pages of comparable tools, and says where each fact comes from.

paragraphs: Michael Serrano describes Rindler as a map of a website that an agent calls instead of reading the page. The map knows the site's screens, what you can do on each and what comes back, so your agent gets the same fields in the same shape every run.

He says the team builds each map once before anyone runs against it: an ingest step works out the site, a mapper drives it click by click to draft the map, and a fleet of agents checks it. They had mapped more than 1,000 sites at launch.
launch_story.attribution: Michael Serrano, maker, on Product Hunt

use_cases: Pulling records or statements from a supplier, carrier or payer portal every week
Checking claim or order status across login-gated sites
Submitting the same form on a portal that has no API
Letting your own agent call a site through Rindler's MCP server

fit: have staff re-keying data from portals that will never have an API
work in procurement, insurance, healthcare billing, recruiting or lending, the use cases its site lists
want predictable structured output rather than a general browsing agent
not_fit: only need occasional one-off scraping: plans start at $100 a month
want a self-serve tool for many sites cheaply: the Starter plan covers one login-gated site

pricing.intro: Rindler charges for runs that finish: one run is one completed task, however many steps it takes. Prices are in US dollars.

plans.name: Starter
plans.detail: 7-day free trial; 100 one-off runs a month; one login-gated site set up with you; access to every supported site; email support

plans.name: Teams
plans.detail: 1,000 runs a month, one-off or scheduled; 10 login-gated sites; scheduled automations; team workspace

plans.name: Enterprise
plans.detail: More sites, extra capacity, annual agreement billed monthly with a pilot first month, dedicated onboarding

notes: 1 run = 1 finished task = $1, according to the pricing page; steps and time don't count.

alternatives.intro: Other tools that automate work in websites. Prices are from each company's own pricing page on 14 October 2026.

items.name: Skyvern
items.what: AI browser automation for forms, portals and workflows
items.difference: A general AI browser agent priced by credits, with an open-source core; Rindler pre-maps each site and charges per finished run.

items.name: Browse AI
items.what: No-code robots that extract and monitor website data
items.difference: Built mainly for scraping and monitoring public data; Rindler focuses on tasks inside login-gated portals.

liked: Consistent fields in the same shape every run
Working with the existing AI ecosystem rather than competing with it
asked: Whether there is an SDK or TypeScript client (use the MCP server over HTTP with a bearer token, the makers said)
What if a site blocks agent access (Rindler works the site the way a person does; there is no API access to grant)
criticised: One commenter warned that a map that falls quietly out of date could return the right shape with wrong values

quotes.text: A map that's quietly a week behind still returns the right shape with a value read off the wrong element
quotes.author: Asad M.

quotes.text: I'm always excited by products that make the entire AI ecosystem stronger rather than competing with every existing tool.
quotes.author: Angela Anna

pros: Works on portals with no API, including behind logins
Rules for actions it must never take, with a log
cons: $100 a month minimum after the trial
The home page now promotes a different product, Maxxwell

x.none: Apart from Rindler's own account, we found no posts on X clearly about the product.

faq.a: A service that runs repetitive web tasks on the portals your team logs into, such as pulling records, downloading statements and submitting forms, from plain-English instructions.
Starter is $100 a month for 100 runs after a 7-day free trial, Teams is $1,000 a month for 1,000 runs, and Enterprise is custom. A run is one finished task.
Founders who met at MIT; the site says it was founded in 2025 and is backed by Y Combinator. On Product Hunt the makers are Michael Serrano and co-founder and CTO Arthur De Los Santos.

faq.q: Can developers call Rindler from code?
faq.a: Yes, through its MCP server over HTTP with a bearer token, according to the makers.

faq.q: What happens when a site changes?
faq.a: Rindler says it maps sites ahead of time and repairs workflows when pages change, and tells you when a run doesn't go through.
